en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 132: The Discourse to Ānanda on the One Who Has Had a Single Excellent Night (Ānandabhaddekarattasutta)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now on that occasion, in the assembly hall, the Venerable Ānanda was instructing, urging, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, reciting the summary and the exposition of “One Fortunate Night.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, who was it that, in the assembly hall, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, and recited the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’?

“Venerable sir, it was the Venerable Ānanda who, in the assembly hall, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, and recited the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night.’”
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“But how, Ānanda, did you instruct, exhort, inspire, and gladden the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, and how did you recite the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’?

“It was in this way, Bhante, that I instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk, and I recited the summary and the exposition of ‘One Fortunate Night’: [Ānanda then proceeded to recite the discourse].
One should not pursue the past,
nor should one long for the future;
what is past has been abandoned.
And that which has not yet been reached, the future;
and whatever phenomenon is present—
whosoever discerns them therein, each in its own place;
Unshakable and unshakeable—
that the wise person should cultivate.
What must be done should be done with diligence this very day.
Who knows when death will come tomorrow?
For we have no appointment with that Death who leads a great army.
One who dwells thus,
ardent and untiring by day and night,
is indeed called "Bhaddekaratta."
The sage, being peaceful, explains:
"And how, friends, does one pursue the past?
One thinks, 'I had such a form in the past,' and thereby brings about delight; 'I had such a feeling in the past'..."
Therein, one relishes it, thinking: "I had such perception in the past"; therein, one relishes it, thinking:
"I had such volitional formations in the past"; therein, one relishes it, thinking: "I had such consciousness in the past."
In this way, friends, one pursues the past.
And how, friends, does one not pursue the past?
One does not bring about delight in regard to the thought, "I had such a form in the past," nor in regard to the thought, "I had such a feeling..."
Regarding the past time, one does not take delight therein: "I had such a perception in the past time"—one does not take delight therein;
"I had such a volitional formation in the past time"—one does not take delight therein;
"I had such a consciousness in the past time"—one does not take delight therein.
In this way, friends, one does not pursue the past.
And how, friends, does one long for the future?
One thinks, "May I be such a person in the future," and thereby brings about delight in that regard; "May I have such feeling... and so forth.
‘May I have such perception in the future… may I have such volitional formations in the future… may I have such consciousness in the future’— one finds delight therein.
In this way, friends, one longs for the future.
And how, friends, does one not long for the future?
One does not bring delight to the thought, "May I be such in the future," nor to the thought, "May I have such feeling... [and so on].
"I might have such perception in the future...
I might have such volitional formations in the future...
I might have such consciousness in the future"—one does not take delight therein.
In this way, friend, one does not long for the future.
And how, friend, is one carried away by present phenomena?

Here, friend, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—[is carried away].
One regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form;
[likewise] feeling … perception …

One regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations... One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self,
or self as being in consciousness— in this way, friend, one is swept away by phenomena regarding the present.
And how, friends, is one not shaken regarding present phenomena?
Here, friends, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the Noble Ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form.
not feeling … not perception … not volitional formations …
One does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in self,
nor self as being in consciousness— in this way, friend, one is not shaken regarding present phenomena.
One should not pursue the past...
One should not long for the future;
that which is past is abandoned,
and that which is yet to come has not been reached.
And whoever discerns, here and there, the phenomenon that is present—
unshakable and unshakeable—
Knowing this, one should apply oneself to it.
Diligence is to be practiced this very day;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no compact with that Death who has a great army;
[we do not fear him] toward one who dwells thus, ardent.
“Unwearied throughout day and night—
him indeed the peaceful Sage calls ‘One Fortunate Night.’”
"In this way, Bhante, I instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a talk on the Dhamma, and I recited the summary and the exposition of 'One Fortunate Night.
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
It is good that you, Ānanda, have instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a talk on the Dhamma, and have recited the summary and the exposition of 'One Fortunate Night.'"
“One should not pursue the past...
That indeed is called ‘one who has had a single auspicious night.’”
“The Sage explains to the virtuous.
And how, Ānanda, does one pursue the past? ... [as before] ...
In this way, Ānanda, one pursues the past.
And how, Ānanda, does one not pursue the past? ... [as before] ...
It is in this way, Ānanda, that one does not pursue the past.
And how, Ānanda, does one look forward to the future? ... [as before] ...
In this way, Ānanda, one looks forward to the future.
And how, Ānanda, does one not look forward to the future?
… [as before] … In this way, Ānanda, one does not look forward to the future.
And how, Ānanda, is one carried away by present phenomena? ... [as before] ...
In this way, Ānanda, one is carried away by present phenomena.
And how, Ānanda, is one not carried away by present phenomena? ... [as before] ...
In this way, Ānanda, one is not shaken regarding present phenomena.
“One should not pursue the past... [as before] ...”
“The Sage who is at peace indeed declares that to be ‘One Fortunate Night.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, elated, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The second discourse, the *Ānanda-bhaddekaratta-sutta*, is finished.
